promptHtml: A Gray-code count changes one bit at each step. Put these five 3-bit values in the order the count takes them, starting from 000.
explanationHtml: From 000, each step changes one bit: 001, 011, 010, then 110. Counting in binary instead, 001 to 010 changes two bits at once, and a synchroniser that caught that change halfway could see 011 or 000: a count one step ahead or one step back, not the one the counter holds. A reader that took 011 for the writer's count would read a place not yet written.

promptHtml: This is afifo, empty, with the read clock rclk drawn as the cycles. The writer stores its first value in cycle 0, on its faster wclk, and its write pointer changes at that edge. rempty is a register on rclk, worked out from the write pointer once the read side's two synchroniser flip-flops have taken it. Set rempty for every cycle.
explanationHtml: The write pointer, in Gray code, reaches the read side through two flip-flops on rclk, which take it at the edges of cycles 1 and 2. rempty is a register worked out from the second, so it falls at the next edge: cycle 3. The reader learns of a new value three of its own edges late, which errs on the safe side: it never reads a place that has not been written.

promptHtml: In afifo, the read side counts in binary in rbin and shows its place to the write side in Gray code. Fill in rgray_next, the Gray code of rbin_next.
explanationHtml: rbin_next ^ (rbin_next >> 1): each bit of the count, exclusive-or the bit above it. Two neighbouring counts then differ in one bit, so the write side's synchroniser, catching a change, sees the old place or the new one. It is the same line as the write side's, with the read side's names.

promptHtml: press_count's two clocks come from one oscillator: clk_b is made from the board's clock inside the FPGA, by its clock manager, the MMCM. So Vivado would time the paths between them. Every such path goes through a synchroniser. Fill in the option that tells Vivado to leave them untimed.
explanationHtml: set_clock_groups -asynchronous puts the clocks in groups whose paths to each other Vivado does not time. That is right only because every crossing is synchronised; a crossing without a synchroniser would then fail on the board with no warning in the timing summary, which is why the CDC report checks each one.

promptHtml: press_count_nogroups is press_count built without its set_clock_groups line. Below is the header of its worst path, which fails.
explanationHtml: 0.125 ns. Without clock groups, Vivado treats the clocks as related, since one is made from the other, and allows the path the closest a clk_b edge comes after a sys_clk_pin edge: 100.125 ns against 100.000. No path is that fast, so it fails. But it runs from level_a into meta_reg, the first flip-flop of a synchroniser, built to take a change at any time; with set_clock_groups Vivado leaves it untimed, and the build meets timing.
